rv.q: This is the very rare play that works better as a star vehicle because it actually furthers the themes of the play.
Give him his due, Hugh Jackman is a damn fine actor.

Those attending simply to ogle Jackman (buff and charismatic as always) get an extra treat, if they can appreciate it: a movie star facing an acting challenge in an exceptional piece of stage writing.

The three-character drama is emotionally exposed and intensely inconclusive -- a poetic, lusty puzzle that rivets one moment, exasperates another, and is destined to keep theatergoers arguing about its meaning all the way home, if not all season.
But despite the considerable charisma and commitment of its outsize star, Hugh Jackman, this new work is a sliver of a mood piece that never tightens its grip.
“The River” is conducted in a more minor key, and is also a more minor effort.
Whether manliness is next to goodliness is a different question, one the play itself — riveting, troubling, thought-provoking, unsatisfying — struggles to embody and never really answers.
The decision to let this sequence drag on so excruciatingly actually guts the work itself.
The too-capacious venue is more ocean than river, and the emotional impact suffers.

Aside from the charismatic star’s intense performance as a lovesick fisherman who is given to poetic laments over the fish (and the woman) who slipped away from him, just about everything else about Jez Butterworth’s strange chamber piece, “The River,” is a downer.

The 85-minute play falls somewhere between thriller and love story, without being sufficiently filling as either; the plot keeps its numerous secrets so close to the vest that it never manages to tantalize, and its characters are too cold to develop feelings for.
But the characters aren’t simply anonymous — they’re ciphers.
There are too many worthier fish in the Broadway sea to bother with this one.
And not only because it's deliberately ambiguous but also because it's great theater: great writing, great acting, great production.

If anyone's ever earned the right to star in a play as a character called-simply-The Man, it is Hugh Jackman. In Jez Butterworth's The River, a mind-bending, occasionally precious, always tense chamber drama, the star wears that moniker proudly...

THE RIVER New Broadway play, at the Circle In the Square, 1633. Broadway. Written by Jez Butterworth. Directed by Ian Rickson. With Hugh Jackman, Cush Jumbo and Laura Donnelly. Schedule: 7 p.m. Tuesday and Thursday; 8 p.m. Friday; 2 and 7 p.m. Wednesday; 2 and 8 p.m. Saturday; 3 p.m. Sunday. Tickets: $35 to $175. 212-239-6200, or telecharge.com.
When Jackman puts it that way, he makes trout-fishing sound a lot like falling in love.
His sturdy star turn is manly, measured and speckled with melancholy.
The same might be said generally for this intriguing but ultimately disappointing play.
While the 85-minute play does offer interesting observations on relationships, mystery and lyrical language, it has a dearth of action.
All that busy work, and Hugh does look impressive in the kitchen; but Butterworth's eighty-five minute play doesn't make for a tasty meal.

Their portentous talk weighs down the fragile twist in the story, and in the end, the never-resolved mystery isn’t so much ambiguous as it is “trickery,” Butterworth’s word for the art of fly-fishing.
Leaving The River, I found myself merely one of the many, many bewildered, shaking my head and speechless.
Not much happens in “The River.”

cn.t: Critics are divided on Butterworth's enigmatic 85-minute drama, with Jackman's intense, charismatic performance earning praise while the play itself frustrates many as thin and gimmicky despite atmospheric staging.

sg.ra: In the 3/4 thrust configuration these front rows put you at the lip of the playing area with actors entering from aisles directly beside you. Headout notes rows AA-B are 'closest to the stage' and audiences are 'roped into the play's action.' Because the stage is surrounded on three sides, the acting is deliberately blocked so no front row gets a sustained back-of-actor view, but individual moments will face away from you — that is inherent to in-the-round and not a flaw of this section.

Universally cited as the optimal vantage in this thrust venue — close enough to feel the intimacy of a 776-seat room with only 10 rows, but one row back from the front so sightlines catch the whole three-sided playing area. Headout: 'Center Orchestra - rows B, C and D' positioned centrally are 'possibly the best seats in the house.' The in-the-round blocking is designed so these central rows at eye-level with the floor see choreography and staging as intended.

Because the venue only has 10 rows total and stadium-inclined seating, rows H-I still feel close to the thrust while giving elevated sightlines that reveal staging patterns on the floor — useful for musicals with choreography. Headout: 'Rows H and I in the upper middle level offer a great view of the stage and the prices are lower than those of the premium orchestra seats.' AVFMS reviewer MusicaltheatreWhiz in H144 (Just in Time, Feb 2026): 'There really isn't a bad seat in the house!' TripAdvisor: 'up is better for musicals.'

In a typical Broadway house the last row would be a skip, but Circle in the Square is only 10 rows deep so row K is roughly where Row G would be in a standard theater. AVFMS danielb9 at K109 (Just in Time, Feb 28 2026): 'Enough legroom to be comfortable and despite being in the back row felt very connected to the action.' Multiple reviews note 'no obstruction' and 'great seat' for row K. Stadium incline ensures sightlines over heads. The in-the-round nature means some scenes still play toward the opposite side, but this is a venue property not a section flaw.

sg.n: Side Sections - Long Arms of the Horseshoe (100s & 200s)
sg.ra: The two long 'wide sides' of the horseshoe (the 100 and 200 numbered sections per BWW forum user Patash's question about 102/202 numbering) give a profile view of the main action. TripAdvisor: 'the two wide sides are fine' and are preferred over 'straight in front' which is 'too far from the rear end of the main stage.' AVFMS samr32 at C207 (Just in Time, Feb 26 2026): 'Amazing seat! Can see both stages so well, and the actors (including Jonathan Groff) run up and down the aisle right near you.' The 300-degree blocking means side sections regularly get face-forward moments; not behind-stage.

The one sustained warning across every source is the extreme corner seats where the horseshoe's ends meet the stage. Headout/TickPick specifically: 'seats 438-440 are obstructed when actors perform on the far left of the stage and vice versa for the opposite side' (437-439). Unlike the rest of the house where in-the-round angles are temporary, these corner positions can have whole extended scenes played entirely out of view on the opposite corner. In a 3/4 thrust with actors using the full perimeter, this is a structural flaw of the seat, not a temporary blocking issue.
